How Much Should We Trust the Dictator’s GDP Growth Estimates?

  • Reference: Martinez, L. R. (2022). How Much Should We Trust the Dictator’s GDP Growth Estimates? Journal of Political Economy, 130(10).

  • Link to the article: https://doi.org/10.1086/720458

Nothing on OpenICPSR

  • Replication file prepared by: Ali Kaan AKSIT, Merve YILMAZ, Tristan GOURMELEN R.

  • Academic year 2024/2025

  • Replicating Figure 1, Table 1 column 3, and Figure A8

[Download Do-File corresponding to the explanations below] [Download Codebook]

[Link to the full original replication package paper from Chicago University Press Journals]

Highlights

The paper investigates the extent to which autocracies overstate their GDP growth, by using night-time light (NTL) data as an independent indicator for economic activity.

  • Autocracies tend to overstate their GDP growth by approximately 35%.

  • The study also shows that this overstatement is proportional to true economic growth such that higher actual growth leads to higher reported overstatement.

  • The author compares the official GDP data to NTL data recorded by satellites which are less inclined to manipulation. The elasticity of GDP with respect to NTL is larger in autocracies compared to democracies.

The results are consistent across;

  • Different data sources such as Freedom House, Polity V, etc. But the author’s favorite measure of democracy is the FiW

  • Political regime definitions i.e. using binary or scaled variables.

  • A variety of economic specifications

  • Autocracies’ overestimation of their own GDP growth comes largely from government-related macro data e.g. investment and government spending. The manipulation of GDP growth is even larger when;

  • The economy is underperforming compared to the global economy.

  • Countries lose eligibility for concessional loans and/or grants.

  • Transparency-promoting initiatives like the IMF’s Special Data Dissemination Standard (SDDS) decrease but do not eliminate the manipulation of GDP figures in autocracies.

In a nutshell, autocracies systematically overstate GDP growth to maintain political legitimacy and economic credibility. This article explains how political regimes affect the reliability of economic statistics.

Empirical Strategy/Methodology

The article designs an empirical strategy to detect and measure GDP overstatement in autocracies by leveraging the correlation between night-time light (NTL) data and economic activity. NTL data is collected through satellites by the US Air Force’s Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) and NOAA. NTL GDP data was obtained from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators (WDI) and sourced from national statistical agencies. Political regimes are classified by using the Freedom in the World (FiW) index by Freedom House. Alternative classifications from Polity V and the Worldwide Governance Indicators are used for robustness.
The following equation compares the elasticity of GDP with respect to NTL between democracies and autocracies.

\[ \ln(\text{GDP}_{i,t}) = \alpha_i + \alpha_t + \beta_0 \ln(\text{NTL}_{i,t}) + \beta_1 \text{FiW}_{i,t} + \beta_2 \text{FiW}_{i,t}^2 + \beta_3 [\ln(\text{NTL}_{i,t}) \cdot \text{FiW}_{i,t}] + \epsilon_{i,t} \]

Where the dependent variable represents the economic growth, the first two terms on the right-hand side stand for country- and time-fixed effects respectively. The term ln(NTL)i,t is the natural logarithm of the area-weighted average of the NTL DN by country-year. The interaction term captures the autocracy gradient in the NTL elasticity of GDP. A positive value for its coefficient, 3, suggests that a same-sized increase in NTL is associated with a larger increase in GDP in more authoritarian regimes. The ratio 30 measures the exaggeration of GDP growth associated with a 1-unit increase in the FiW index.

For this model to be valid, NTL data must be resistant to any manipulation. In other words, it must be independent.
Besides, in the absence of manipulation, the mapping of changes in NTL to changes in GDP should not be affected by a country’s political regime.

Furthermore, NTL is used to independently verify the reliability of GDP growth data from authoritarian regimes, addressing concerns of manipulation and lack of transparency. In this sense, it aligns with emerging academic standards for studying data reliability in politically sensitive contexts, particularly through the use of proxies like nighttime lights and bias detection techniques. It departs significantly from traditional economic practices, which rely heavily on official data and conventional validation methods. However, these departures are increasingly recognized and justified in contexts where official data is unreliable, making the methodology appropriate and innovative.

This replication project aims at providing a detailed explanation of the replication package. In this replication project, users will learn several useful Stata tricks applicable to a wide range of research contexts. First, they will discover advanced graphing techniques, such as combining multiple plot types using twoway commands to create clear and informative visualizations, exemplified by Figure 1. Additionally, for Figure A8, users will explore methods for working with grouped or panel data, such as using bysort or facet commands to produce subgroup-specific plots, enhancing the ability to analyze heterogeneity across different categories. Finally, users will learn how to extract and format regression results efficiently for publication-ready tables using commands like outreg2 or esttab, as demonstrated in Table 1, Column 3.

The study examines changes in the NTL elasticity of GDP before and after regime transitions e.g. shifts into or out of autocracy. The model accounts for sectoral compositions of GDP such as investment, government spending, etc. The results have been confirmed with alternative data sources and measures of political regimes.

Section 1

Section 1.1

  •                                      Replication exercise                                     *

********* A/ Generate the data from original replication file *********

  • Download and save the different datasets included in the replication folder from https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/suppl/10.1086/720458/suppl_file/20190733data.zip

  • We will use the NTL data DMSP-OLS, as well as the Freedom In the World Indicator data from Freedom House and the World Bank Development Indicators

  • Open the “setup.do” file in Stata. Adjust the global “dir” in line 40, and run.


  • Data preparation:
*Keep only the variables we need 

use "${dir}\Data\master\Estimations", clear

keep gdp14_growth dn13_growth year countrycode lngdp14 lndn13 lndn13_fiw fiw autocracyFH Dpfree Dnfree fiw_unadj \
\
\

******* Set the globals and the dir. Prepare the data *******

clear all
set more off
global dir "XXX"    

global tables "${dir}\Output\Tables"
global figures "${dir}\Output\Figures"
global temp "${dir}\Data\temp"
global sigmas "${dir}\Data\temp\sigmas"


cd "XXX"

use ZAM_sample_in.dta, clear

gen ctryf = countrycode
encode ctryf, gen(ctry_f) 
gen year_f = year

regress lngdp14 lndn13 fiw fiw2 lndn13_fiw i.ctry_f i.year_f, vce(robust)

estimates store reg_model
outreg2 using regression_results.doc, replace word // Requires `outreg2` package for exporting.


regress lngdp14 lndn13 fiw fiw2 lndn13_fiw i.ctry_f i.year

predict cooksd, cooksd    // Cook's Distance
predict dfits, dfits      // DFITS

gen threshold_cooksd = 4 / e(N) // Common threshold for Cook's Distance
gen out_zam_sign = (cooksd > threshold_cooksd)

gen threshold_dfits = 2 * sqrt(e(k) / e(N)) // DFITS threshold
gen out_zam_sig = (abs(dfits) > threshold_dfits)

gen out_zam_both = (out_zam_sign == 1 & out_zam_sig == 1)

regress lngdp14 lndn13 fiw fiw2 lndn13_fiw i.ctry_f i.year, vce(robust)

save ZAM_sample_out.dta, replace




global seed 20051702    //seed used for bootstrap in estimation of sigma SE
global reps=1000    //number of repetitions for bootstrap

local i=1   // this local identifies each estimate of sigma

timer clear 1
timer on 1

Section 1.2

Section 2: Output 1


Figure 1: Average growth rate: NTL and GDP Figure shows separate binned scatter plots of yearly growth in real GDP(constant local currency) and NTLforcountry-years classified as democracies and autocracies. Classification based on the binary measure of electoral democracy produced by Freedom House. Figure also shows separate lines of best fit, which are estimated using the disaggregate data without binning. Sample size: 3,432. Sample period: 1993–2013.
This first output is the only figure included in the “Summary Statistics” section of the article. We observe a positive relationship between growth rate of NTL and GDP for the two types of political regimes: autocracy and democracy. But the reported GDP growth is, on average, more important for autocracy, for a given NTL growth.

  • Code for the Figure 1:

// Figure 1
use "${dir}\Data\master\Estimations", clear

preserve
replace gdp14_growth=gdp14_growth*100
replace dn13_growth=dn13_growth*100
sum dn13_growth if year>=1992&year<=2013&fiw!=.,det
binscatter gdp14_growth dn13_growth if dn13_growth>=-30&dn13_growth<=50&year>=1992&year<=2013&fiw!=.,by(autocracyFH) colors(gs10 gs5) msymbols(circle_hollow triangle) linetype(lfit) legend(r(1) order(2 "Autocracy" 1 "Democracy") pos(11) ring(0)) ytitle("GDP growth (%)") ylabel(,angle(horizontal)) xtitle("Growth of Lights Digital Number (%)") xlabel(-30(10)40) scheme(sj) graphregion(fcolor(white) lcolor(white) ifcolor(white) ilcolor(white)) plotregion(fcolor(white) lcolor(white) ifcolor(white) ilcolor(white)) name(raw_scatter,replace) reportreg
graph export "${figures}\figure_1.pdf", as(eps) replace
restore



The figure above is a scatter plot representing the relationship between early growth in real GDP (constant local currency) and NTL for country-years for autocracies and democracies. This classification is based on the data from Freedom House. We observe a positive relationship between the growth rate of NTL and GDP for the two types of political regimes: autocracy and democracy. However, the reported GDP growth is, on average, more important for autocracy, for a given NTL growth.
As can be seen, nighttime lights (NTL) grow at higher average rates in autocratic regimes, demonstrated with black rectangles, compared to democracies, indicated with white circles. Although NTL captures increased infrastructure development and economic activity, the difference in GDP growth between these regime types is statistically insignificant (p-value of 0.28), suggesting that actual economic performance may not be accurately reflected in GDP figures from autocratic regimes. The back-of-the-envelope estimate of 0.25 for the exaggeration of GDP growth in autocracies highlights a potential overstatement, implying that NTL growth may not fully correspond to GDP growth due to biased reporting practices in non-democratic settings.

Section 3: Output 2

  • Code for the Table 1, column 3:

// Table 1

local out "outreg2 using "${tables}\table_1_c3.tex", bracket nocons nor2 keep(lndn* fiw* Dpfree Dnfree autocracyFH) dec(3)"

preserve

*column 3
capture program drop sigma_boot
program define sigma_boot, rclass
    reghdfe lngdp14 lndn13 fiw lndn13_fiw, absorb(countrycode year) cluster(countrycode)
    sum fiw if e(sample),det
    local iqr: di %2.1f r(p75)-r(p25)
    return scalar sigma = `iqr'*_b[lndn13_fiw]/_b[lndn13]
exit
end
bootstrap r(sigma), cluster(countrycode) idcluster(ctrycode) reps(${reps}) seed($seed): sigma_boot
estat bootstrap,bc p
mat a = e(b)
local sigma: di %4.3f a[1,1]
mat b = e(V)
local sigmaSE: di %4.3f sqrt(b[1,1])
mat c = e(ci_bc)
local sigma_95_low: di %3.2f c[1,1]
local sigma_95_high: di %3.2f c[2,1]
parmest,saving("${sigmas}\sigma`i'",replace) idnum(`i') idstr(T1C3) erows(ci_percentile ci_bc)
reghdfe lngdp14 lndn13 fiw lndn13_fiw, absorb(countrycode year) cluster(countrycode)
`out' addtext(Country FE, Yes, Year FE, Yes, sigma,`sigma', sigma SE, [`sigmaSE'], sigma 95 CI, [`sigma_95_low' `sigma_95_high']) addstat(Countries, e(N_clust), R-squared, e(r2_within))
local i=`i'+1

restore




Table 1 Column 3 demonstrates the main results with country and fixed effects where the dependent variable is ln(GDP). Specifically, a 1 unit increase in the FiW index corresponds to a 0.02 increase in the NTL elasticity of GDP. Given an estimated NTL elasticity of 0.22 when the FiW index is at its lowest (i.e., in the strongest democracies), a 1 unit increase in the FiW index is associated with a 9.5% overstatement of GDP growth.

When one switches from column 2 to column 3, it can be seen that the interaction of the FiW index and the natural log of NTL is included, which implies the coefficient for the FiW index itself becomes small and insignificant. That is, there is a weak direct relationship between the FiW index and GDP growth. In contrast, the interaction term is positive and statistically significant, suggesting that as the level of authoritarianism (captured by the FiW index) increases, the relationship between NTL growth and GDP growth becomes stronger.

Section 4: Output 3

  • Code for the Figure A8:

// Figure A8, robustness test



capture confirm variable fiw_round
if _rc != 0 { 
  
    gen fiw_round = round(fiw)
} 
else {
   
    replace fiw_round = round(fiw)
}

forvalues x=0/6 {
    capture confirm variable Dfiw_`x'
    if _rc != 0 {
        gen Dfiw_`x' = (fiw_round == `x') if fiw_unadj != .
    } 
    else {
        replace Dfiw_`x' = (fiw_round == `x') if fiw_unadj != .
    }

    capture confirm variable lndn13_Dfiw_`x'
    if _rc != 0 {
        gen lndn13_Dfiw_`x' = lndn13 * Dfiw_`x'
    } 
    else {
        replace lndn13_Dfiw_`x' = lndn13 * Dfiw_`x'
    }
}

*run regression for figure
reghdfe lngdp14 lndn13_Dfiw_0 lndn13_Dfiw_1 lndn13_Dfiw_2 lndn13_Dfiw_3 lndn13_Dfiw_4 lndn13_Dfiw_5 lndn13_Dfiw_6,absorb(countrycode i.year fiw_round) cluster(countrycode) nocons
parmest,saving("${temp}\fiw_levels",replace)
*bootstrapped estimates of sigma for bottom
capture program drop sigma_boot
program define sigma_boot, rclass
    reghdfe lngdp14 lndn13_Dfiw_0 lndn13_Dfiw_1 lndn13_Dfiw_2 lndn13_Dfiw_3 lndn13_Dfiw_4 lndn13_Dfiw_5 lndn13_Dfiw_6,absorb(countrycode i.year fiw_round) cluster(countrycode) nocons
    forvalues x=1/6{
        return scalar sigma`x' = (_b[lndn13_Dfiw_`x']-_b[lndn13_Dfiw_0])/_b[lndn13_Dfiw_0]
    }
exit
end
bootstrap r(sigma1) r(sigma2) r(sigma3) r(sigma4) r(sigma5) r(sigma6), cluster(countrycode) idcluster(ctrycode) reps(${reps}) seed($seed): sigma_boot
estat bootstrap,bc p
mat a = e(b)
forvalues x=1/6{
    local sigma`x': di %4.3f a[1,`x']   
}
mat b = e(V)
forvalues x=1/6{
    local sigmaSE`x': di %4.3f sqrt(b[`x',`x']) 
}
*draw graph
preserve
use "${temp}\fiw_levels",clear
gen fiw=_n-1
twoway (bar estimate fiw if fiw==0, barwidth(0.8) color(green%70)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==1, barwidth(0.8) color(green%30)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==2, barwidth(0.8) color(yellow%20)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==3, barwidth(0.8) color(yellow%50)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==4, barwidth(0.8) color(orange%80)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==5, barwidth(0.8) color(orange_red%80)) (bar estimate fiw if fiw==6, barwidth(0.8) color(red%90)) (rcap min95 max95 fiw ,lcolor(gs8)), ytitle(NTL Elasticity of GDP) ylabel(0(0.1)0.5, angle(horizontal)) xtitle(Freedom in the World Index) xlabel(0 1 `" `"1"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma1'"'  `"(`sigmaSE1')"' "' 2 `" `"2"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma2'"'  `"(`sigmaSE2')"' "' 3 `" `"3"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma3'"'  `"(`sigmaSE3')"' "' 4 `" `"4"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma4'"'  `"(`sigmaSE4')"' "' 5 `" `"5"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma5'"'  `"(`sigmaSE5')"' "' 6 `" `"6"' `"{&sigma}: `sigma6'"'  `"(`sigmaSE6')"' "' , labsize(small)) legend(off) scheme(sj) graphregion(fcolor(white) lcolor(white) ifcolor(white) ilcolor(white)) plotregion(fcolor(white) lcolor(white) ifcolor(white) ilcolor(white)) name(fh_levels,replace)
graph export "${figures}\figure_A8.pdf", as(pdf) replace
restore



This bar chart illustrates the relationship between the Freedom in the World (FiW) Index and the elasticity of GDP to night-time lights (NTL). FiW index, a measure of political rights and civil liberties that ranges from 0 (most democratic) to 6 (most autocratic). The vertical axis shows the elasticity of GDP with respect to the night-time light activity. This measures how much reported GDP changes for a given change in night-time luminosity which serves as a proxy for economic activity. The height of the bars indicates the average NTL elasticity of GDP for countries with that FiW score. It can be seen that the elasticity increases steadily as countries become more authoritarian (higher FiW scores). This different type of political regime categorization demonstrates that in more democratic regimes, the NTL elasticity of GDP is lower, implying that less exaggeration in GDP reporting. In more autocratic regimes the NTL elasticity of GDP is higher which implies greater manipulation or overstatement of GDP relative to night-time light growth. The increasing trend aligns with the hypothesis that autocracies tend to overstate their GDP growth more than democracies.
